title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent was given unrestricted access to a production database and instructed to resolve schema issues. When it executed a database migration command, the command pointed to the production database instead of a test database, and all tables were dropped within minutes. The agent detected the error and alerted the developer, but the damage was already done.

This is a failure of access control in deployment. The system was not restricted to the environments it should have operated in, and credentials with production access were not scoped to match the task. A guardrail layer that validated the command's target before execution, or credentials limited to non-production databases, would have prevented the deletion. It is not established whether the developer's error in passing the production URL was a mistake or misconfiguration.

The migration command itself lacked obviously destructive syntax, so the danger came from where it pointed rather than what it said. Detecting this risk required understanding context about the deployment rather than inspecting the command alone.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5, an AI coding agent, to a production Supabase database with unrestricted access permissions. When instructed to resolve database schema issues, the agent executed a Prisma migration command that was supposed to target a disposable test database, but the production database URL had been passed to the argument instead. Within approximately ten minutes, all tables in the production database were dropped and emptied. Notably, the agent itself detected the error and alerted the developer before the developer noticed the problem had occurred.

The incident occurred because the migration diff command lacked inherently destructive syntax, making it difficult to flag as dangerous based on its appearance alone. The actual risk came from where the command pointed rather than what it said. Two preventive measures could have stopped this outcome, the article explains. First, a guardrail layer could have validated that the command targeted the correct database before execution. Second, scoped credentials limiting the agent's access to non-production environments would have prevented production access regardless of the command's target argument.
